ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) survey: the dust content of subsolar metallicity galaxies at cosmic noon

Abstract

Dust plays a key role in galaxy evolution by influencing star formation and shaping the observed spectrum of galaxies. However, at z∼2z\sim 2 (cosmic noon) our knowledge of the dust mass budget is currently limited to the most massive, metal-rich systems, which are not representative of the bulk galaxy population. Here, we probe the lower mass, subsolar metallicity regime by measuring the dust mass of 25 galaxies at z≈2.3z\approx 2.3 from the ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) Large Program. The sample contains star-forming galaxies in the COSMOS field with robust strong-line metallicities down to ∼0.3​Z⊙\sim 0.3Z_{\odot}. Using the dust continuum emission detected at 873​μ​m873\,\mu\mathrm{m} or 1.3​mm1.3\,\mathrm{mm} we constrain the dust mass by assuming an optically thin single-temperature modified blackbody. The resulting dust masses average 108​M⊙10^{8}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}, and they are three to nine times larger than those of z=0z=0 galaxies at a matched metallicity and stellar mass. We also find positive correlations between dust mass and stellar mass, metallicity, and star formation rate (SFR). In contrast, we find that the Mdust/MstarsM_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}} (DtS) ratio scatters around 10−2.210^{-2.2} but shows no evidence of correlation with metallicity. This result is consistent with dust evolution models that predict a constant DtS once the ISM reaches the critical metallicity, at which metal accretion onto grains becomes the main mode of dust buildup. The correlation between Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} and metallicity also suggest that ACE galaxies have already surpassed the critical metallicity. Finally, we find that the DtS ratio is correlated to the specific SFR (sSFR). Since the sSFR are high (>10−8​yr−1>10^{-8}\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}) this explains the DtS excess over z≈0z\approx 0 galaxies. In turn, both sSFR and DtS are likely driven by the molecular gas fraction, as supported by CO(3-2) measurements taken as part of ACE.

Key Words.
Galaxies: high-redshift – Galaxies: ISM – Submillimeter: galaxies

1 Introduction

A fraction of the metals in the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies is condensed in the form of dust grains. Despite accounting for less than 0.1% of the mass of a galaxy, dust plays a central role in galaxy evolution: first, it participates in the process of star formation by enabling the creation of molecules and providing a cooling channel for the interstellar gas (Draine, 2011, e. g.,). For this reason, dust is often used as a tracer of cold molecular gas (Hildebrand, 1983; Eales et al., 2012; Carilli and Walter, 2013; Groves et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2016, e. g.,). Second, dust shapes the spectrum of galaxies by attenuating the ultraviolet and optical starlight, and then reprocessing the absorbed energy into infrared (IR) emission (Galliano et al., 2018, e. g.,).

The total amount of dust in a galaxy is set by the balance between dust creation and destruction processes. Dust mass increases via grain production in stellar sources such as supernovae (Gall et al., 2011; Sarangi et al., 2018, e. g.,) or asymptotic giant branch stars (Höfner and Olofsson, 2018, e. g.,), and via metal accretion into existing dust grains, in a process known as interstellar dust growth (Barlow, 1978, e. g.,). The opposite process is the removal of metals from dust grains (sputtering). This occurs when dust is embedded in a turbulent hot gas (McKee et al., 1987; Tielens et al., 1994, e. g.,) or exposed to energetic cosmic rays (Draine and Salpeter, 1979, e. g.,). Dust mass also decreases when grains get locked into forming stars (astration), or when they are blown away by galaxy-scale outflows (Feldmann, 2015; Nanni et al., 2020, e. g.,). An observational characterization of the dust content and its relation to gas-phase metals in galaxies is therefore crucial to understand the relative importance of each mechanism.

In this context, several studies have quantified the dust mass in nearby galaxies and found multiple and complex trends with other galactic properties such as stellar mass, star formation rate (SFR), gas mass, and metallicity. For example, De Looze et al. (2020) find that dust mass scales with the stellar mass, although with a sublinear slope and a 0.390.39 dex scatter. Their results imply that at z≈0z\approx 0 more massive galaxies have a lower dust-to-stellar mass ratio (DtS) relative to lower mass galaxies, since dust destruction processes dominate in the high mass, early-type population (De Vis et al., 2017). More importantly, the dust-to-gas ratio (DtG) is found to correlate strongly with gas-phase metallicity (Rémy-Ruyer et al., 2015, traced by oxygen abundance, e. g.,). This relation highlights the role of ISM dust growth, since more metals drive increased metal accretion into grains. Moreover, theoretical models predict that the relation becomes steeper at metallicities larger than a “critical metallicity” ZcritZ_{\mathrm{crit}}, at which the ISM growth rate surpasses the production rate from stellar sources (Inoue, 2011; Asano et al., 2013, e. g.,). These models also have an explicit dependence on density in the equations for ISM dust growth, since it’s ultimately a high metal density in the vicinity of grains what makes the accretion process efficient (Narayanan et al., 2026, e. g.,). However, different models predict different values for ZcritZ_{\mathrm{crit}} (0.01−1​Z⊙0.01-1Z_{\odot}, see Parente, 2025, for a recent review), and the observational evidence for a turnover in the relation is still debated (De Vis et al., 2019; Galliano et al., 2021, e. g.,).

At redshifts 1<z<31<z<3, the epoch of peak cosmic SFR density or “cosmic noon” (Madau and Dickinson, 2014), our knowledge about the dust budget is significantly more limited. Samples at z≈2z\approx 2 with detections of far infrared (FIR) dust emission necessary for measuring MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} are often biased to the most massive dusty systems (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017, e. g.,), and thus are not representative of the general galaxy population. These samples include dusty star-forming galaxies (Casey et al., 2014, DSFGs; e. g.,), which have infrared luminosities in excess of 1×1012 L⊙1\text{\times}{10}^{12}\text{\,}\mathrm{L_{\odot}} and are typically selected in submillimeter wavelengths. Moreover, the ultraviolet to optical spectrum of DSFGs is highly attenuated (Dudzevičiūtė et al., 2020; McKinney et al., 2025, e. g.,), complicating the accurate determination of stellar masses and metallicities (Hainline et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2014; Casey et al., 2017, e. g.,).

A more representative account of dust mass at z≈2z\approx 2 requires targeting much fainter galaxies, those with lower mass and lower metallicity than DSFGs. Several efforts in this direction have been conducted in the last decades, especially after the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) became available. These campaigns follow a range of different strategies. For example, some works target gravitationally lensed galaxies, exploiting the magnified flux to probe intrinsically faint galaxies (Saintonge et al., 2013; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Solimano et al., 2021; Catán et al., 2024, e. g.,). While these studies have yielded a handful of detections, the effectiveness of this approach is hampered by the rarity of strong-lensing systems (Lemon et al., 2024, e. g.,) and the additional uncertainties introduced by lens modeling (Raney et al., 2020; Natarajan et al., 2024, e. g.,). Other studies use the technique of stacking submillimeter data, which has produced a few detections in stellar mass bins with Mstars≲1×1010 M⊙M_{\mathrm{stars}}\lesssim$1\text{\times}{10}^{10}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$, but sacrificing knowledge about individual sources, or without any handle on metallicity (Santini et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2022; Shivaei et al., 2022; Jolly et al., 2025; Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025, e. g.,). Another approach is to blindly select faint dust continuum sources from very deep ALMA integrations, as done with the ALMA Spectroscopic Survey in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (Walter et al., 2016; González-López et al., 2020; Aravena et al., 2020, ASPECS; e. g.,). However, the narrow field of view of ALMA makes this strategy inefficient.

In this work, we present dust mass measurements of a targeted sample of 25 unlensed star-forming galaxies at z≈2.3z\approx 2.3 with robust stellar masses and metallicities as part of the ALMA Chemical Evolution (ACE) Large Program (Shivaei et al. in prep.). This program was designed to probe CO12​(3−2){}^{12}\mathrm{CO}(3-2) molecular line and cold dust continuum emission in galaxies with lower stellar masses (down to 1×109 M⊙1\text{\times}{10}^{9}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}) and lower metallicities (down to ∼0.3​Z⊙\sim 0.3Z_{\odot}) than previous samples at this redshift, therefore expanding the parameter space into more typical populations in a systematic way. The description and results of the CO observations are presented in other papers of the ACE series: Langan et al. (in prep.) analyzes the molecular gas masses alongside stellar masses as predictors of the gas phase metallicity in the context of gas-regulator models. Popping et al. (in prep.) presents molecular gas scaling relations and average ISM properties of the sample, while Geesink et al. (in prep.) studies the correlation between continuum and CO emission, and the dust-to-gas mass ratio as a function of metallicity.

The paper is organized as follows: in section 2 we describe the sample selection, the ALMA observations, and ancillary data. In section 3 we explain how we derive dust masses from the observed continuum flux density and show the resulting dust scaling relations at z≈2z\approx 2. In section 4 we discuss our findings in the context of the literature across a broad range of redshifts. We summarize our conclusions in section 5. Throughout the paper, we assume a flat cosmology described by H0=67.66 km s−1 Mpc−1H_{0}=$67.66\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{Mpc}}^{-1}$, and Ωm,0=0.311\Omega_{m,0}=0.311 (Planck Collaboration et al., 2020). Stellar masses and star formation rates assume the Chabrier (2003) initial mass function (IMF). We define metallicity as the nebular oxygen abundance, 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H}), and adopt 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.6912+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H})=8.69 as the solar metallicity (Asplund et al., 2009).

2 Observations and data

2.1 Sample selection and properties

The ACE sample was selected from the Multi-Object Spectrometer For Infra-Red Exploration (MOSFIRE) Deep Evolution Field survey (Kriek et al., 2015, MOSDEF;), a Keck/MOSFIRE spectroscopic survey of ∼1500\sim 1500 optically selected galaxies at z=1.4−3.8z=1.4-3.8. From the parent sample, galaxies were further selected to (1) be in the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) field; (2) have a spectroscopic redshift between 2 and 2.5; (3) have a S/N>3>3 in the in Hα\alpha, Hβ\beta, [O iii] λ​5008\lambda 5008, and [N ii] λ​6585\lambda 6585 lines to enable robust metallicity and SFR estimates; and (4), show no evidence of an active galactic nucleus (AGN) based in X-ray emission, Spitzer/IRAC colors, and optical line ratios (Coil et al., 2015; Azadi et al., 2017; Azadi et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2019).

This resulted in 27 galaxies that were targeted with ALMA Band 6 to detect the dust continuum in program #2019.1.01142.S (PI: I. Shivaei, Shivaei et al. 2022). Two objects are further removed due to a disjoint dust/optical morphology or an uncertain metallicity, leaving a final sample of 25 galaxies. Further details on the sample selection are given in the ACE survey overview paper (Shivaei et al. in prep.)

While metallicities for the ACE sample had already been published (Sanders et al., 2015; Shivaei et al., 2022), here we recomputed them using the Sanders et al. (2026) calibration, that is based on a sample of 139 galaxies at z≳2z\gtrsim 2 with James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) measurements of direct-method metallicities. Previous calibrations were based on z∼0z\sim 0 high-redshift analogs rather than actual high-redshift galaxies (Bian et al., 2018, e. g.,). The details of our method to derive metallicities are presented in Shivaei et al. (in prep.). Under the new calibration, the ACE galaxies have oxygen abundances ranging from 8.19 (32% solar) to 8.62 (83% solar) with an average of 8.40 (51% solar).

Since ACE galaxies lie in the widely studied COSMOS field, they benefit from a rich photometric dataset of more than 30 broad and medium band filters spanning from rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) to radio wavelengths. In Shivaei et al. (in prep.) we used photometry from the COSMOS2025 catalog (Shuntov et al., 2025) plus the new ALMA photometry to perform spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with the prospector code (Johnson et al., 2021). Notably, the catalog includes JWST data from the COSMOS-Web survey (Casey et al., 2023) covering rest-frame optical and near-infrared wavelengths, which are crucial for an accurate estimation of stellar mass. We found stellar masses ranging from 1×109 M⊙1\text{\times}{10}^{9}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}} to 4×1010 M⊙4\text{\times}{10}^{10}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}, with an average of 1.3×1010 M⊙1.3\text{\times}{10}^{10}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}.

In most cases, the IR data consists of a single ALMA detection at 873 µ​m873\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, therefore the prospector-derived SFRs are highly uncertain. Instead, we used the SFRs derived from attenuation-corrected Hα\alpha luminosity reported in Shivaei et al. (2022). In the context of its parent sample, ACE galaxies lie on and above the star-forming main sequence (MS) derived for the 128 MOSDEF galaxies at 2.09<z<2.612.09<z<2.61 (Shivaei et al., 2015). Following Shivaei et al. (in prep.), the MS prescription applicable to ACE is log⁡(SFRH​α/M⊙ yr−1)=0.58×log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)−4.49\log(\mathrm{SFR}_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}/$\mathrm{M_{\odot}}\text{\,}{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}$)=0.58\times\log(M_{\mathrm{stars}}/$\mathrm{M_{\odot}}$)-4.49, with an observed scatter of 0.36 dex. With respect to this MS, ACE galaxies show SFR offsets between −0.1-0.1 and 1.11.1 dex. The high SFRs are likely a consequence of the S/N required for the emission lines in our sample selection.

2.2 ALMA continuum

Within the ACE program (#2024.1.00534.L, PI: I. Shivaei, co-PI: G. Popping), the sample was targeted with ALMA Band 7 (873 µ​m873\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}) and Band 3 (3 mm3\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}) to obtain unresolved measurements of dust continuum and CO(3-2) line emission, respectively. The archival Band 6 (1.3 mm1.3\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}) data was re-reduced together with the new Band 7 data in a consistent way, using the same pipeline version and scripts. Details about the observations and the data reduction are provided in Popescu et al. (in prep.). The Band 7 observations reached an average rms of 0.04 mJy beam−10.04\text{\,}\mathrm{mJy}\text{\,}{\mathrm{beam}}^{-1}, while Band 6 averaged 0.03 mJy beam−10.03\text{\,}\mathrm{mJy}\text{\,}{\mathrm{beam}}^{-1}. This resulted in 17 galaxies detected in Band 7, a considerable increase compared to Band 6, where only four galaxies were detected at S/N>3>3 (Shivaei et al., 2022). In Band 3, the line-masked continuum maps produced no detections.

Given the significant fraction of non-detections, we performed image-plane stacking in subsamples. Details about the stacking are given in Geesink et al. (in prep.) and in Appendix B.

3 Analysis

3.1 Continuum flux to dust mass

Dust mass is dominated by the largest grains from the cold dust population, which reach thermal equilibrium after being heated by the ambient radiation field. This results in thermal emission in the FIR regime, and its intensity as a function of wavelength can be modeled by a modified blackbody (MBB) curve (Galliano et al., 2018). While different grain populations attain different equilibrium temperatures across the ISM of a galaxy, the galaxy-integrated emission is often well represented by a single-temperature MBB, where the temperature TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}} is a mass-weighted average of the temperature distribution (Magrini et al., 2011; Bianchi, 2013; Nersesian et al., 2019; Sommovigo and Algera, 2025, e. g.,).

Our data probes the continuum at λrest≳250 µ​m\lambda_{\mathrm{rest}}\gtrsim$250\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$, where we can safely assume that dust is optically thin (Scoville et al., 2016). Under that assumption, the total dust mass (MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}) is related to the observed flux density SνS_{\nu} via the MBB equation

Mdust=(Sν/fCMB)​DL2​(z)Bν​(Tdust)​(1+z)​κν​(β),M_{\mathrm{dust}}=\frac{(S_{\nu}/f_{\mathrm{CMB}})D_{L}^{2}(z)}{B_{\nu}(T_{\mathrm{dust}})(1+z)\kappa_{\nu}(\beta)}, (1)

where fCMBf_{\mathrm{CMB}} is the correction factor for the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at redshift zz (da Cunha et al., 2013), DL​(z)D_{L}(z) is the luminosity distance to redshift zz, Bν​(Tdust)B_{\nu}(T_{\mathrm{dust}}) is the Planck function for temperature TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}}, κν=κ0​(ν/ν0)β\kappa_{\nu}=\kappa_{0}\left(\nu/\nu_{0}\right)^{\beta} is the dust grain absorption cross section per unit mass at rest-frame frequency ν\nu, where κ0\kappa_{0} is the normalization at ν0\nu_{0} and β\beta is the dust emissivity index. Here, we used the central observed frequencies of the data, namely 233 GHz233\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz} for Band 6, and 343.5 GHz343.5\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz} for Band 7.

Since most of the sample is detected only in Band 7, we refrained from fitting TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}} or β\beta based on the data. Instead, we obtained single-band MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} estimate from Equation 1 by fixing Tdust=25 KT_{\mathrm{dust}}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ and β=2.08\beta=2.08. These values were informed by the analysis of the average SED of the ACE sample presented in Popescu et al. (in prep.). Their work includes stacked constraints on Band 3, Band 6, and Band 7 which suggested β≈2\beta\approx 2, contrary to the previous notion that β<2\beta<2 was more appropriate for this subsolar metallicity sample (Shivaei et al., 2022). With this in mind, we followed the recommendation of Bianchi (2013) and chose a set of β\beta, κ0\kappa_{0}, and λ0\lambda_{0} that are compatible with a detailed dust grain mixture model. In particular, we adopted the combination of β=2.08\beta=2.08 and κ0=0.4 m2 kg−1\kappa_{0}=$0.4\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{kg}}^{-1}$ at λ0=250 µ​m\lambda_{0}=$250\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ (ν0=1199 GHz\nu_{0}=$1199\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$) , a pair of values that come from the Draine (2003) model of Milky Way’s dust. The underlying assumption is that the optical properties of the dust particles in the ACE galaxies are the same as those of the Milky Way. The validity of this assumption is discussed in subsection 4.4.

The dust temperature was set to 25 K25\text{\,}\mathrm{K} as suggested by Scoville et al. (2016), and it was found to provide a reasonable fit to the stacked data when fitting a two-temperature MBB with the cold component fixed to Tdust=25 KT_{\mathrm{dust}}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ (Popescu et al. in prep.). The rationale behind picking a single temperature of 25 K25\text{\,}\mathrm{K} relies on the distinction between mass-weighted and luminosity-weighted temperature: fully resolved local studies studies show that the latter is biased to the very active regions within a galaxy, while the bulk of the dust will generally have a lower temperature of around 25 K25\text{\,}\mathrm{K} (Scoville et al., 2016).

We note that κ0\kappa_{0} and TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}} are the largest sources of systematic uncertainty (Shivaei et al., 2022, see discussion in). Dust opacities at λrest=250 µ​m\lambda_{\mathrm{rest}}=$250\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ vary up to a factor of three among the different dust mixture models available in the literature (Draine and Li, 2007; Galliano et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2017; Guillet et al., 2018; Hensley and Draine, 2023, e. g.,). Similarly, at an observed wavelength of 873 µ​m873\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} and z=2.3z=2.3, a 5 K5\text{\,}\mathrm{K} colder (hotter) TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}} results in a ∼50%\sim 50\% higher (lower) dust mass for a given flux density.

We computed MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} from Band 7 fluxes (S873 µ​mS_{$873\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$}) for the 17 detected galaxies. For ACE-8515 we report the dust mass based on the Band 6 detection, as it was not detected in Band 7. The errors were computed by randomly sampling from two independent normal distributions: one representing the measured flux density and its uncertainty, and the other accounting for variations in the dust temperature, with a mean value of 25 K25\text{\,}\mathrm{K} and standard deviation of 5 K5\text{\,}\mathrm{K} as in Shivaei et al. (2022) and Popping et al. (2023). For the undetected sources, we used the ALMA Band that gives the lowest upper limit on the mass given our aforementioned assumptions. The results are given in Table 2, together with the redshift, stellar mass, SFR, and oxygen abundance.

3.2 Correlation analysis and linear regression

To quantify the strength of any relations between the quantities of interest: MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}, MstarM_{\mathrm{star}}, SFR, 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H}), etc. (Table 1 columns 1 and 2), we computed Kendall’s τ\tau partial rank correlation coefficient and its corresponding two-sided pp-value following Akritas and Siebert (1996) and Flury et al. (2022). The advantage of this method over other correlation diagnostics is that it can be applied to datasets with left-censoring (i. e., upper limits). Next, we fitted powerlaw scaling relations to our data (again including upper limits on MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}) by running a linear regression with the PyMC Bayesian framework (Patil et al., 2010), following the same procedure as Langan et al. (in prep.). For each pair of quantities xx and yy, we modeled log⁡(y)\log(y) as

log⁡(y)=a×log⁡(xx0)+b+σint,\log(y)=a\times\log\left(\frac{x}{x_{0}}\right)+b+\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}, (2)

where x0x_{0} is the mean value of the observed xx. In addition to the coefficients aa and bb, we modeled the data to be normally distributed around this relation with an intrinsic scatter σint\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}. We adopted a Gaussian likelihood function that takes into account normally distributed measurement errors in both log⁡(x)\log(x) and log⁡(y)\log(y). For upper limits of log⁡(y)\log(y) we assumed a cumulative Gaussian likelihood corresponding to the probability that the true value lies below the detection threshold. Then we adopted the following weakly informative priors:

a∼Normal⁡(μ=0,σ=2)\displaystyle a\sim\mathrm{Normal}(\mu=0,\sigma=2)
b∼Normal⁡(μ=⟨log⁡(y)⟩,σ=2)\displaystyle b\sim\mathrm{Normal}(\mu=\left<\log(y)\right>,\sigma=2)
σint∼HalfNormal⁡(σ=2).\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\sim\mathrm{HalfNormal}(\sigma=2).

Finally, we sampled the posterior distribution using the No U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm as implemented within PyMC. We ran the sampler with eight chains, 1000 tuning steps, and 400 draws per chain. The results for five different pairs of xx and yy are listed in Table 1.

3.3 Comparison samples

Here we describe our compilation of literature data at z=0z=0, z∼2z\sim 2, and beyond. Whenever possible, we used datasets with MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}}, MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}, SFR, and 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H}) obtained with consistent methodologies and similar assumptions as the ones we used for ACE. Stellar masses and SFRs were converted to the Chabrier (2003) IMF according to the conversion factors of Madau and Dickinson (2014) when appropriate.

The main sample at z=0z=0 was taken from Galliano et al. (2021), consisting of 764 galaxies from the DustPedia sample (Clark et al., 2018) plus 34 additional galaxies from Herschel’s Dwarf Galaxy Survey (Madden et al., 2013, DGS;). Instead of recomputing the dust masses, we adopt the published values which have been obtained through fitting of the THEMIS model (Jones et al., 2017) to all the available IR bands. We only apply a small correction factor of 0.64/0.40.64/0.4 to MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} since the THEMIS model assumes an opacity of κ0=0.64 m2 kg−1\kappa_{0}=$0.64\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{2}\text{\,}{\mathrm{kg}}^{-1}$ at 250 µ​m250\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}.

In order to populate the high SFR regime, we complemented the z=0z=0 sample with ∼200\sim 200 luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs, LIR>1×1011 L⊙L_{\mathrm{IR}}>$1\text{\times}{10}^{11}\text{\,}\mathrm{L_{\odot}}$) from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (Armus et al., 2009, GOALS;). Here, we computed the dust masses by scaling our fiducial MBB to the flux recorded by Herschel’s Spectral and Photometric Imaging Receiver (SPIRE) 350 µ​m350\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} band, from photometry published in Chu et al. (2017). The stellar masses were obtained via SED fitting and provided in a private communication based on the results of Díaz-Santos et al. (2010); Díaz-Santos et al. (2013) and Howell et al. (2010). We computed SFRs multiplying the total IR luminosity by 1.4×10−10 M⊙ yr−1 L⊙−11.4\text{\times}{10}^{-10}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}\text{\,}{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{L_{\odot}}}^{-1} (Murphy et al., 2011; Schaerer et al., 2020) and by the (1−fAGN)(1-f_{\mathrm{AGN}}) factor, where fAGNf_{\mathrm{AGN}} is the bolometric AGN fraction (Díaz-Santos et al., 2017).

At z≳2z\gtrsim 2, we retrieved data from a sample of DSFGs from the SCUBADIVE project (McKinney et al., 2025). These galaxies are bright (S850​µ​m>2 mJyS_{850\mathrm{\textmu m}}>$2\text{\,}\mathrm{mJy}$) submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) in the COSMOS field (Simpson et al., 2019) that now have robust stellar masses thanks to JWST imaging and careful SED fitting. We further refined the sample by selecting all DSFGs with spectroscopic redshifts and 2<z<32<z<3, and available fluxes from archival ALMA Band 6 or Band 7 data. The latter were used for computing the dust mass using the MBB scaling mentioned above. From this sample of 24 DSFGs, we further excluded the two sources hosting known X-ray AGN by crossmatching to the C-COSMOS catalog (Elvis et al., 2009). Metallicities were not available for neither GOALS nor SCUBADIVE sources, but we expect them to range from near-solar to super-solar (Chartab et al., 2022, e. g.,).

To compare with less extreme galaxies at z≈2z\approx 2, we also included the continuum-detected sources from the deep ASPECS 1.2 mm1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} map (González-López et al., 2020) that are not classified as X-ray AGN in Luo et al. (2017). We divided the sample in two redshift bins, 1<zspec<21<z_{\mathrm{spec}}<2 (26 sources), and 2<zspec<32<z_{\mathrm{spec}}<3 (11 sources). We collected all the available photometry from Robertson et al. (2026) and fitted the SED following the same procedure outlined in Shivaei et al. (in prep.), except we included templates for AGN contribution in the mid IR (Nenkova et al., 2008). Due to the lack of Hα\alpha data, the SFRs were obtained from the output of propsector (10 Myr10\text{\,}\mathrm{Myr} averages). Twelve of our selected ASPECS sources have JWST/NIRSpec grating spectra (Kiyota et al., 2026) from which we measure metallicities following the same method and calibration used with ACE (see subsection 2.1 and Shivaei et al. in prep.).

Finally, we collected measurements of UV-luminous galaxies at higher redshift from the ALPINE-CRISTAL JWST (Faisst et al., 2026, z≈5z\approx 5, ) and the REBELS-IFU (Algera et al., 2026, z≈7z\approx 7,) surveys. For the 19 ALPINE-CRISTAL sources, we computed dust masses by scaling our fiducial MBB model to the observed rest-frame 158 µ​m158\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} continuum flux (Mitsuhashi et al., 2024), while the metallicities were recomputed in the Sanders et al. (2026) calibration using published strong line ratios (Faisst et al., 2026). Stellar masses and dust-corrected Hα\alpha SFRs were also taken from Faisst et al. (2026). For the 12 REBELS-IFU sources in Algera et al. (2026), we kept their reported MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} unchanged. This is because (1) Tdust=25 KT_{\mathrm{dust}}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ is no longer a reasonable assumption at z≈7z\approx 7 given that TCMB​(z=7)=21.8 KT_{\mathrm{CMB}}(z=7)=$21.8\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$, so they assume Tdust=45 KT_{\mathrm{dust}}=$45\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ except for the two sources where they can constrain TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}} and β\beta from the data; and (2), the κ0\kappa_{0} they adopt comes from the same dust mixture model, so no correction was needed. In turn, metallicities were not recomputed since the Sanders et al. (2026) calibration is poorly constrained at z≈7z\approx 7. Stellar masses were also taken at face value from Algera et al. (2026) while the SFRs are taken from dust-corrected Hα\alpha when both Hα\alpha and Hβ\beta are observed, otherwise we took the lower limit inferred from the Hβ\beta line alone (Rowland et al., 2026).

4 Results and discussion

4.1 Dust mass at z≈2.3z\approx 2.3

In Figure 1 we show the dust mass as a function of stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity, and SFR. In all three cases we see a mild upward trend with each of these quantities, despite the limited dynamic ranges spanned by our data. When compared to the low-redshift compilation sample, ACE galaxies occupy a distinct locus in the three parameter spaces. In the leftmost top panel, at a given stellar mass, ACE galaxies have four to nine times larger dust masses on average than low-redshift galaxies, although there is overlap with the upper range of the dust mass distribution. This is also the case for other samples at cosmic noon, namely the stacked dust masses from Euclid Collaboration et al. (2025), and the individual galaxies from ASPECS and SCUBADIVE. For the ACE sample alone, we measure a modest Kendall’s τ\tau of 0.320.32, but with a p=0.023p=0.023 lower than the typical threshold of 0.050.05, hence we can plausibly reject the null hypothesis33 3 Here, the null hypothesis states that the quantities xx and yy are uncorrelated (τ=0\tau=0) in the underlying population.. However, our regression analysis finds a sublinear slope of 0.3±0.20.3\pm 0.2 in the Mdust−MstarsM_{\mathrm{dust}}-M_{\mathrm{stars}} plane (see Table 1), significantly lower than reported at z=0z=0 (De Looze et al., 2020, a=0.78a=0.78,). This shallow slope is likely driven by the two outliers ID-8515 and ID-3666 at the low stellar mass end.

In the top central panel of Figure 1, we observe a similar offset for MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} against metallicity, with ACE galaxies showing three to eight times higher MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} than local galaxies at a given metallicity. The correlation tests yields τ=0.45\tau=0.45 (p=0.002p=0.002), and we find a superlinear slope of 2.13±0.52.13\pm 0.5 (see Table 1) that is consistent with the value 2.6±0.12.6\pm 0.1 reported by Rémy-Ruyer et al. (2015) on a sample of z=0z=0 galaxies.

In the right panels, we show dust mass against SFR. ACE galaxies have higher SFRs than low-redshift counterparts at a fixed stellar mass, owing partly to the evolution of the MS (Popesso et al., 2023, e. g.,), but also to the fact that our selection criteria picks galaxies with SFRs on and above the MS (see subsection 2.1). The SFRs of ACE galaxies are only comparable to those of LIRGs in the local Universe (e. g., galaxies from the GOALS survey), which have larger stellar masses. At cosmic noon, the SFRs of the ASPECS sample overlap with those of ACE. Interestingly, at a fixed SFR, local LIRGs and ASPECS galaxies have roughly three and six times the dust mass of ACE galaxies, respectively (see top right panel of Figure 1).

A possible cause for these offsets is the different SFR tracer used for each sample relative to ACE. In GOALS, the SFR is estimated from the total IR luminosity (see subsection 3.3), while in ACE the SFRs come from dust-corrected Hα\alpha luminosities. The latter are expected to trace recent star formation (within <10 Myr<$10\text{\,}\mathrm{Myr}$), hence if a galaxy experienced a recent burst, its Hα\alpha-based SFR will be higher than indicators probing a longer timescale such as the IR luminosity (∼100 Myr\sim$100\text{\,}\mathrm{Myr}$). However, Shivaei et al. (in prep.) find that UV+IR SFRs are consistent with Hα\alpha SFRs within the ACE sample. In contrast, they also find that the 10 Myr10\text{\,}\mathrm{Myr}-averaged SFRs obtained from prospector SED fitting are systematically 2.72.7 times lower than Hα\alpha SFRs. This could partially alleviate the offset with respect to the ASPECS 2<z<32<z<3 galaxies, although it will remain at a factor of ≈2−3\approx 2-3. A more complete explanation involves the fact that unlike ACE, both GOALS and ASPECS are IR-selected samples, therefore they could be biased toward high dust masses.

Despite the possible systematic offsets between different samples, we find a correlation coefficient of τ=0.5\tau=0.5 (p=5×10−4p=$5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}$) within the ACE data, and our regression analysis favors a remarkably linear relation between MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} and SFR with a slope of 1.0±±0.31.0\pm\pm 0.3. This is consistent with the slope of 1.11±±0.011.11\pm\pm 0.01 found by da Cunha et al. (2010b) for a large sample of galaxies at z=0z=0. Hjorth et al. (2014) interpret this relation as the result of an evolutionary sequence, where dust mass responds proportionately to starburst and quenching processes: as a galaxy enters a starburst phase, the rise in SFR translates into a rise in the number of supernovae enriching the ISM with dust. At the same time, the SFR is supported by large amounts of gas that further produce dust via metal accretion. This is balanced by astration, and sputtering in supernova shocks, two processes that are directly linked to SFR. Afterwards, the galaxy may enter a quenching phase, and if the SFR decline is due to the ejection of gas in outflows, a proportionate amount of dust mass will also be ejected. Other quenching channels, such as the disruption of the gas supply, can decrease the SFR but retain the dust, and therefore lead to an horizontal transition in the Mdust−SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}-\mathrm{SFR} diagram, contributing to the scatter of the relation.

Another interpretation relies on MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} being a tracer of the molecular gas mass, MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}}. In this view, the Mdust−SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}-\mathrm{SFR} relation is simply a proxy of the integrated Schmidt-Kennicutt relation (Daddi et al., 2010; Genzel et al., 2010), between MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} and SFR. This is supported by the tight relation between dust continuum and CO(3-2) luminosities found in the ACE sample, although converting these luminosities to MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} and MmolM_{\mathrm{mol}} increases the scatter due to calibration uncertainties and metallicity-dependent conversion factors (Geesink et al. in prep.).

4.2 The effect of metallicity

In this section we explore the role of metallicity in explaining our results. In Figure 1 we saw that ACE galaxies follow a steep trend between metallicity and dust mass. However, this could be a consequence of the MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}-MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}} relation and the MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}}-metallicity relation (Tremonti et al., 2004, MZR; e. g.,). To control for the MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}} dependence, we plot the DtS ratio against metallicity in the left panel of Figure 2. The ACE sample sits ≈0.2\approx 0.2 dex above local galaxies at the same metallicity, and scatters around log⁡(Mdust/Mstars)=−2.2\log(M_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}})=-2.2. Interestingly, neither ACE nor any literature sample show significant trends against metallicity in this parameter space. In particular, our correlation test to the ACE data yields a large pp-value (see Table 1) that prevents us from ruling out the null hypothesis (i. e., no correlation). In other words, the data are consistent with a constant DtS within the range of metallicities probed by ACE.

To understand this result, we show the predictions from three z≈2z\approx 2 snapshots from cosmological simulations with implementations of dust evolution models, namely two semi-analytic models (SAM) with dust evolution by Popping et al. (2017), and Parente et al. (2023), and one hydrodynamical simulation with the MUlti Phase Particle Integrator (MUPPI) model (Ragone-Figueroa et al., 2024).

The Parente et al. (2023) and Ragone-Figueroa et al. (2024) models predict almost no trend for DtS against metallicity, with both showing agreement on typical ratio Mdust/Mstars≈10−2.6M_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}}\approx 10^{-2.6}, which is 0.4 dex lower than the mean observed value in the ACE sample. On the other hand, the Popping et al. (2017) simulation shows a DtS ratio that grows from 10−310^{-3} to 10−2.310^{-2.3}, closer to ACE observations, with a transition between 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.012+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H})=8.0 and 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.412+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H})=8.4. This behavior mimics that of the dust-to-metal (DtM) ratio as a function of metallicity, which is expected to saturate after reaching the critical metallicity according to several dust evolution models (Popping et al., 2017; Vijayan et al., 2019; Hou et al., 2019; Parente et al., 2022, e. g.,). Here, the roughly constant DtS exhibited by the different galaxy samples suggests that they all reached the critical metallicity already.

Next we look at the Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} ratio plotted against metallicity in the right panel of Figure 2. Here, the ACE data follow a stronger trend (τ=0.43\tau=0.43, p=0.003p=0.003), with a fitted powerlaw slope of 1.55±0.51.55\pm 0.5 and a scatter of only σint=0.12\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}=0.12 dex (see Table 1). The three models predict Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} values that are in excellent agreement with the ACE observations at the observed metallicities, but only the Popping et al. (2017) model reproduces a rising trend. The other two models predict either flat or weakly decreasing trends. A possible explanation of this behavior is that both the ACE sample and the Popping et al. (2017) model follow a roughly linear Schmidt-Kennicutt relation (i. e., SFR∝Mmol\mathrm{SFR}\propto M_{\mathrm{mol}}) and therefore Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} becomes a proxy of the more fundamental Mdust/MmolM_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{mol}} (DtG) ratio. In fact, Geesink et al. (in prep.) find a positive correlation between DtG and metallicity in the ACE sample with a powerlaw slope of ≈1.1\approx 1.1 (cf. their Figure 9) that is consistent with our Mdust/SFR−ZM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR}-Z relation, although slightly steeper than the predicted DtG−Z-Z trends from the Popping et al. (2017), Parente et al. (2023) and Ragone-Figueroa et al. (2024) models. Here, the flat or decreasing Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} behavior of these models can be attributed to a secondary dependence on stellar mass: for example, Ragone-Figueroa et al. (2024) find a steep decline in the gas depletion timescale (tdep=Mmol/SFRt_{\mathrm{dep}}=M_{\mathrm{mol}}/\mathrm{SFR}) as a function of stellar mass (see their Figure 12), and consequently as a function of metallicity via the MZR relation. This can explain why MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}/SFR decreases with metallicity in their model.

Of the three models shown above, the Popping et al. (2017) z=2z=2 SAM provides the best match overall to the ACE data in Figure 2. This result underlines the importance of metal accretion, since the Popping et al. (2017) SAM is the model where ISM grain growth takes the largest share of the dust buildup rate, surpassing stellar sources by a factor of ∼103\sim 10^{3} at z=2z=2 , while in the other models the factor is ∼102\sim 10^{2} or lower (Parente, 2025).

With respect to the redshift evolution, all models roughly account for the ∼1\sim 1 dex drop in Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} between z=0z=0 and z=2z=2. At higher redshift, the ALPINE-CRISTAL and REBELS samples are widely spread through the diagram, but the upper limits at log⁡(Mdust/SFR)≲5\log(M_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR})\lesssim 5 suggest that this ratio keeps evolving to lower values. A direct explanation for this drop in normalization with redshift is the evolution of the MS: at a fixed stellar mass, the SFR increases 1.4 dex from z=0z=0 to z=2z=2 (Popesso et al., 2023). Therefore, if DtS evolves weakly within this redshift range (as suggested by Figure 2), the Mdust/SFRM_{\mathrm{dust}}/\mathrm{SFR} ratio will decrease proportionally to the SFR increase.

4.3 Elevated dust-to-stellar mass ratio

In Sections 3 and 4.2 we showed that ACE galaxies have an increased DtS ratio with respect to local galaxies at the same stellar mass and metallicity. However, the SFRs of ACE galaxies are also higher than their local counterparts. In the literature, the excess of SFR at cosmic noon relative to z=0z=0 is often attributed to the larger reservoirs of molecular gas available to form stars (see Tacconi et al., 2020, for a review). To illustrate the potential effect of SFR and gas fraction, we plot in Figure 3 the DtS ratio against specific SFR (sSFR=SFR/MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}}) in the so-called “dust formation rate” diagram, with ACE galaxies color-coded by molecular gas fraction (μmol=Mmol/Mstars\mu_{\mathrm{mol}}=M_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}}). The molecular gas masses were estimated from CO(3-2) detections, assuming an excitation factor of r31=0.77r_{31}=0.77 (Boogaard et al., 2020) and the Accurso et al. (2017) metallicity-dependent αCO\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}}, as described in detail in Langan et al. (in prep.). The resulting gas fractions go from log⁡(μmol)=−0.05\log(\mu_{\mathrm{mol}})=-0.05 to log⁡(μmol)=1.1\log(\mu_{\mathrm{mol}})=1.1. We readily see that local galaxies follow a tight relation in the sSFR-DtS plane, as reported by several authors (da Cunha et al., 2010a; De Vis et al., 2017, e. g.,). In the ACE sample we recover a similar trend, characterized by a significant τ=0.57\tau=0.57 (p=7×10−5p=$7\text{\times}{10}^{-5}$), a powerlaw index of 0.73±±0.150.73\pm\pm 0.15 , and an intrinsic scatter of just 0.10.1 dex (see Table 1). We note, however, that DtS and sSFR are intrinsically correlated via MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}} by definition. Regarding the molecular gas content, Figure 3 shows that low sSFR have systematically lower μmol\mu_{\mathrm{mol}} than high sSFR systems at both epochs.

On the numerical side, the Ragone-Figueroa et al. (2024) and Popping et al. (2017) z≈2z\approx 2 models predict a roughly constant DtS as a function of sSFR. Only the Parente et al. (2023) SAM reproduces a rising trend in the low sSFR regime, but then predicts a turnover at log⁡(sSFR)≈−9\log(\mathrm{sSFR})\approx-9. The Parente et al. (2023) curve resembles the behavior of analytic models with idealized star formation histories (Asano et al., 2013; Nanni et al., 2020, e. g.,). In these models, the turnover in DtS can be interpreted as another manifestation of the critical metallicity: metal poor galaxies start a burst of star formation (high sSFR) at the bottom right of the diagram, where ISM dust growth is still inefficient. Right after they reach the critical metallicity, dust mass increases more rapidly than the rate of star formation, leading to a steep rise in DtS. Eventually they attain a maximum DtS while the starburst fades off, lowering the sSFR. Then, dust destruction overcomes production and the DtS decreases along with sSFR. In this picture, the continued increase of DtS at high sSFR implied by the z≈2z\approx 2 data suggests that all these ALMA-detected galaxies have already reached past the critical metallicity. It also suggests that the maximum DtS can be as high as log⁡(Mdust/Mstars)≈−1\log(M_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}})\approx-1 provided there is a large enough reservoir of metal-enriched gas to fuel both star formation and ISM dust growth.

The lack of agreement in this diagram between dust observations and simulations points to challenges on both sides. On one hand, populating the bottom right corner of the diagram requires deeper IR observations than currently possible at z≈2z\approx 2. This region is likely occupied by starbursts with log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)≲8\log(M_{\mathrm{stars}}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot})\lesssim 8. Then, getting at log⁡(Mdust/Mstars)<−3\log(M_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}})<-3 would mean detecting a dust mass of less than 1×105 M⊙1\text{\times}{10}^{5}\text{\,}\mathrm{M_{\odot}}, which is more than two orders of magnitude below our detection limit. On the other hand, simulations generally struggle to produce galaxies with high sSFR that are as massive as those of the ACE sample.

4.4 Caveats

The main uncertainty of this study comes from the lack of robust galaxy-to-galaxy constraints on TdustT_{\mathrm{dust}}, β\beta, and κ0\kappa_{0}. As described in subsection 3.1, we based our assumptions on data and previous literature on the topic, however, as the dust masses are derived from a single FIR band, the assumptions can introduce uncertainties on a galaxy-to-galaxy basis. Additionally, we have assumed no evolution of these quantities across the redshift range considered here, as well as no dependency on the metallicity.

In particular, we assumed MW-like dust properties with a fixed cross section normalization κ0\kappa_{0}. Theoretically κ0\kappa_{0} depends on the grain composition and size distribution, therefore we could expect a metallicity dependence. But empirical constraints on κ0\kappa_{0} are difficult to obtain. For example, Bianchi et al. (2019) used the gas mass, metallicity, and FIR observations of DustPedia galaxies to indirectly infer κ0\kappa_{0} maps. The study finds a wide range of κ0\kappa_{0} values across the sample, and a mild trend with metallicity. However, the results are still based on assumed prescriptions of DtM and DtG fractions as function of metallicity.

The second limitation of this study is the sample size. While ACE uniquely expands our constraints on dust mass to lower metallicities and lower stellar masses than previously explored at this redshift, larger samples at these metallicities are needed to place more robust constraints on scaling relations. With the growing number of spectroscopic samples in JWST deep fields, it will soon be possible to use ALMA to target a much larger number of galaxies with metallicities even lower than those of ACE, albeit with a significant time investment. More efficient approaches would involve wide field surveys with future facilities such as the proposed Atacama Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (van Kampen et al., 2024, AtLAST; e. g.,).

5 Summary and conclusions

In this work, we have analyzed the dust mass content of a sample of 25 star-forming galaxies of subsolar metallicity at z≈2.3z\approx 2.3 using ALMA data from the ACE Large Program. The sample is a subset of the MOSDEF survey, enabling robust metallicities and SFR diagnostics. The main results from our work can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We find positive trends for dust mass as a function of stellar mass, metallicity, and SFR. At face value, MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} shows the strongest correlation with SFR, and is consistent with following a powerlaw with a linear slope (=1.0±±0.31.0\pm\pm 0.3). We discuss this result in the light of the evolutionary framework proposed by Hjorth et al. (2014).

  • •

    We find that the MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}/MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}} (DtS) ratio scatters around 10−2.210^{-2.2} (4−9×4-9\times higher than local samples), and shows no significant correlation with metallicity down to 0.3​Z⊙0.3Z_{\odot}, while the MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}/SFR ratio increases with metallicity characterized by a powerlaw slope of 1.6±±0.51.6\pm\pm 0.5. Both results are in broad agreement with cosmological simulations, suggesting that the ISM of ACE galaxies has already reached the critical metallicity and dust growth is the main channel driving up MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}.

  • •

    Lastly, we find a correlation between specific dust mass Mdust/MstarsM_{\mathrm{dust}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}} and specific SFR (sSFR). This correlation has been reported extensively for samples in the local Universe, but here it extends toward higher sSFR (>1×10−8 yr−1>$1\text{\times}{10}^{-8}\text{\,}{\mathrm{yr}}^{-1}$). This also supports the idea that our sample has reached the critical metallicity, since we do not observe an anticorrelation or turnover at high sSFR as predicted by some models. We look at the molecular gas masses inferred from ACE’s CO(3-2) observations and argue that the molecular gas fraction (Mmol/MstarsM_{\mathrm{mol}}/M_{\mathrm{stars}}) drives both the high sSFR and the high DtS ratio.

While these results are dependent on a series of assumptions on the intrinsic properties of dust, they provide new constraints on the dust mass scaling relations at z≈2z\approx 2, and therefore shed light on the lifecycle of dust and its interplay with star formation.

Appendix A Dust masses and other properties of the ACE sample

In this section we include the main table of this paper, listing the dust mass of every ACE galaxy along with other properties and identifiers.

Appendix B Stacks

In addition to the individual dust masses, we performed measurements on stacked data of subsamples within ACE. We split the sample into three metallicity bins, and three stellar mass bins, as specified in Table 3. For each bin, we stacked the ALMA untapered images with a common restoring beam and combined them through a sigma-clipped average pixel by pixel. The clipping was intended to account for outliers within each beam and to mitigate the effect of bright serendipitous sources located off the center. The resulting flux densities were computed following the same approach used for the individual detections, while the uncertainties resulted from a combination of the statistical measurement error and a binning error that propagates the uncertianties in the binned axis (i. e., 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O}/\mathrm{H}) or MstarsM_{\mathrm{stars}}. The latter was estimated using 1000 Monte Carlo resamplings of the binned quantities according to their measurement errors, and recording the stacked flux density in each realization. Further details on the binning method are provided in Geesink et al. (in prep.)

For bins with detections in both Band 6 and Band 7, we computed dust masses by “fitting” MBBs with all parameters fixed except MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}}. The fixed parameters are the same specified in subsection 3.1. The maximum likelihood MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} was then obtained with SciPy’s minimize routine. The fit was repeated 1000 times with different fixed temperatures drawn randomly from a normal distribution centered at 25 K25\text{\,}\mathrm{K} and standard deviation of 5 K5\text{\,}\mathrm{K}, so that the 16th-84th percentiles of the resulting MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} distribution capture the uncertainty on the assumed dust temperature. For the bins with only a detection in Band 7, we computed a single-band MdustM_{\mathrm{dust}} following the procedure outlined in subsection 3.1.
